title: When the Harvest Turns
premise: Dominic Ishikawa, a documentarian of the unmapped, discovers tunnels beneath their hometown that no survey records — and at the mouth of one, the imaginary friend they buried at age nine, still waiting, unchanged. The friend, Wren, is a fragment of something older that was fed in 1974, when the town's founding families traded a child's name for an endless harvest, and Dominic's grandmother helped carry the bargain. As frost spreads in patterns that spell out debts, Dominic must uncover what was taken — a girl named Ada Voss, erased from every record and memory but the tunnels' — and return her name to the town before the first hard frost completes the pattern and claims a new payment: Dominic themselves. In the end, Dominic gives up their own documented identity, their archive, their name in the record, to restore Ada's, surviving as someone unrecorded — free, and unremembered.
about_author: Vesper Almeida is the pen name of a former municipal archivist who spent six years cataloguing property records from rural counties before turning to horror. They write in winter, by lamplight, and claim they have never once gone back to check whether a door was really locked.

chapters.title: The Survey That Isn't
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. An urban explorer with a compulsive documentation habit, Dominic maps a storm drain that extends far beyond any official survey, finding hand-carved tally marks dating back decades. The emotional beat is professional thrill curdling into unease as the tunnel's geometry refuses to match their measurements.

chapters.title: Wren on the Porch
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Returning home at dawn, Dominic finds their childhood imaginary friend sitting on the porch steps — unchanged after twenty-five years, patient as furniture. Wren says only, 'You found the door.' The beat is dread wrapped in terrible nostalgia.

chapters.title: Everything Documented
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic reviews their own archive obsessively — photos, recordings, field notes — searching for rational explanations while Wren watches from the yard without ever seeming to move between glances. The beat is the erosion of a mind built on evidence.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Ledger
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. In their late grandmother's house, Dominic finds a farm ledger from 1974 with pages cut out and a pressed frost-fern pattern burned into the cover. A neighbor mentions, unprompted, 'Your gran always paid early.' The beat is inherited guilt surfacing.

chapters.title: The Tally Marks Count Down
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Re-entering the tunnels, Dominic finds new tally marks beside the old ones — fresh, wet, counting down toward a final stroke. Wren appears deeper inside, closer than the dark should allow. The beat is the realization that the countdown has a deadline: first frost.

chapters.title: What the Town Won't Say
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Dominic and elderly shopkeeper Ruth Ellery. Ruth half-remembers a bad year in '74 — a harvest too perfect, a family that left overnight — but the memory slides away like ice underfoot whenever she reaches for it. The beat is the horror of engineered forgetting.

chapters.title: Frost Writing Itself
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Frost blooms across Dominic's windows in deliberate, fern-like script — the same pattern as the ledger's burn mark. Photographing it, Dominic realizes each image shows different words. The beat is being addressed directly by something patient and enormous.

chapters.title: The Missing Girl
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV, with archival excerpts. Digging through county records, Dominic finds a gap: a 1974 school photo with one face blurred by water damage, and a class list where one line reads only 'V—'. The beat is the first solid clue: someone was taken, not traded willingly.

chapters.title: Wren Remembers Being Real
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Wren finally speaks at length, revealing fragments: they were made from a real child's discarded imagination, given shape by whatever lives below. They don't want to hurt Dominic; they were sent to collect. The beat is sympathy for a thing designed as an instrument.

chapters.title: The Founding Families' Dinner
chapters.summary: Ruth Ellery's POV, breaking open. Under pressure from Dominic's questions, Ruth's suppressed memories rupture: five families in a root cellar in October 1974, a bargain spoken aloud, a nine-year-old girl named Ada Voss handed over so the frost would spare the crops. The beat is confession as wound.

chapters.title: Ada Voss, Erased
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Every trace of Ada — records, gravestones, memories — unravels as Dominic investigates; even photographs of her decay in real time. Only the tunnels hold her, because the thing below keeps what it's owed. The beat is grief for someone the world was made to forget.

chapters.title: The Harvest That Never Fails
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The town's fields stand impossibly green in late autumn while everything around them browns; farmers speak of their luck in flat, rehearsed voices. Dominic sees neighbors glance at the frost patterns on their own doors and look away. The beat is complicity as a communal condition.

chapters.title: Down Where the Names Are Kept
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Guided by Wren, Dominic descends past the mapped sections into a cavern where names hang like preserved fruit — thousands of them, including Ada's, shriveled and dark. Touching one, Dominic hears its owner's whole life in a second. The beat is awe weaponized into terror.

chapters.title: The Price of Looking Away
chapters.summary: Ruth Ellery's POV. Ruth confronts her own role — she was Ada's best friend and chose, at nine, to keep quiet about what the adults did. The thing below offers her a trade: her remaining years for silence. She refuses, and her garden dies overnight. The beat is the cost of refusal.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Deciphering the frost-script fully, Dominic learns the terms: the bargain can be undone only if what was taken is returned willingly by a descendant of those who gave it — and Dominic's grandmother signed. The deadline is the first hard frost, four days out. The beat is a trap disguised as a remedy.

chapters.title: The Archive Burns Cold
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. The thing below makes its counteroffer: Dominic's life and identity in exchange for leaving Ada buried and the harvest intact. Frost consumes Dominic's entire archive — twenty-five years of documentation — page by page, as a demonstration. The beat is watching your selfhood held hostage.

chapters.title: First Frost Eve
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Dominic and Ruth. The town prepares unknowingly for the final payment; Wren stands at the tunnel mouth, weeping without knowing why. Ruth gives Dominic her testimony, written down, the first honest record in fifty years. The beat is grim resolve on the edge of the deadline.

chapters.title: The Descent
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic goes down alone, carrying Ada's reconstructed name — assembled from Ruth's memory, a hymnal inscription, and one surviving photograph. The tunnels reshape around them, testing, offering exits that lead home. The beat is walking into the dark on purpose.

chapters.title: Before the Thing Below
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. In the cavern of names, Dominic faces the entity — vast, agricultural, neither cruel nor kind, merely owed. It explains the arithmetic of survival: something must always be given. The beat is the climax of the theme: power that corrupts by making victims negotiate.

chapters.title: A Name Returned
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic speaks Ada Voss's full name into the cavern and offers their own archive — every record, every proof they existed — as the balancing payment. Ada's name unfurls, bright and whole; the frost-patterns stop mid-stroke. The beat is sacrifice as restoration.

chapters.title: Unrecorded
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV, fragmented. Dominic wakes on the surface as the first frost falls harmless on brown fields. No documents bear their name; Ruth looks at them with warm blankness; Wren is gone, or perhaps finally free. The beat is liberation that feels like erasure.

chapters.title: The New Prayer
chapters.summary: Unnamed narrator's POV, implied to be Dominic. Living unnamed at the town's edge, the narrator begins a new kind of documentation — not to prove existence, but to remember others: Ada's story, Ruth's testimony, the truth of 1974. The last line: some things are kept better outside the ledger. The beat is quiet, earned hope.
